title: Increasing cost of youth sports forcing kids to choose between one or the other at early age
summary: If the rising cost of youth sports pushes athletes to specialize early, it might also endanger two familiar athletic archetypes – the late bloomer and the multisport standout.

image.caption: A recent study of Canadian participation in sports showed that 48 per cent of respondents identified cost as the factor keeping them on the sideline. (Martin Rose/Bongarts/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Isadora Merraro-Sinclair is moving full-speed toward a decision that could affect her for decades.

She’s a strong student with a long and diverse list of outside-the-classroom interests. Her schedule includes music lessons, as well as track and basketball practice. She excels at all three pursuits, but they each consume a lot of hours and dollars, straining her parents’s ability to budget money and time.

Three years ago Isadora’s older sister, Georgia, faced the same crossroads, and dropped out of martial arts classes to focus on volleyball. And by this summer, Isadora’s parents say they’ll likely have to sit down with her to figure out which activity to specialize in.
At age 11.

If that seems like an early age to foreclose on extracurricular options, it’s also par for the modern youth sports course, where rising costs make pursuing multiple disciplines difficult. In response, some families, like the Merraro-Sinclairs, make big decisions about sports specialization fairly in their kids’ careers, hoping to save time and stretch their youth sports dollars.
“At the end of this year we’ll have to make some decisions about time and money, about what she’s going to dig deep on,” says Bridget Sinclair, Isadora and Georgia’s mom.
A New Game Plan: How high a price is pay to play sports?

But if dollar figures illustrate the price of youth sports, the Merraro-Sinclair family also represents some of the hidden costs. Where focusing on one sport as a pre-teen boosts short-term development, experts say sampling different sports yields greater long-range results. And early specialization doesn’t account for intangibles, like whether an athlete’s preferred sport might change, or, crucially, what kind of athlete that child will become post-puberty.
Put another way, if the rising cost of youth sports pushes athletes to specialize early, it might also endanger two familiar athletic archetypes — the late bloomer and the multisport standout.

Isadora and Georgia’s dad, Marlon Merraro, falls into that second category. As a high schooler he played football in the fall and ran track in the spring. Over the winter he wrestled, and even won a city title representing Downsview Collegiate Institute. For him, middle school was a time to try new sports, so he could figure out where to focus his energy in high school.
“I don’t believe any kid should be specializing at 11 years old,” he says.
Many families borrow money to cover costs

Last October, Canadian Tire’s Jumpstart Foundation published an in-depth study about the cost of youth sports in Canada, and unveiled a sobering series of statistics. When researchers ranked the top three reasons that kids don’t play sports, “too expensive” topped the list, with 48 per cent of respondents identifying costs as the factor keeping them on the sideline. Among respondents with kids in organized sport, 32 per cent said they borrowed money to cover costs, and 23 per cent said they worked overtime or picked up a second job to finance their children’s sports careers.

The study also found a strong correlation between the cost of a sport and the number of participants. Soccer had more registered athletes than any other sport, but the median annual cost to register — $460 — landed at the lower end of the cost spectrum.
Youth volleyball can cost up to $4,000 a year between expenses for coaching, registration and travel. (Rebecca S. Gratz/Associated Press)
“The pattern is clear,” the report reads. “The sports with the broadest participation tend to be those with the lowest barriers to entry.”

Behind the numbers laid out in the report are sports parents like Laura Jean-Louis of Brampton. Her three kids range in age from seven to 16. The two oldest are multisport athletes, and all three participate in track and field, where annual registration fees run roughly $800. But when you factor in the cost of shoes, uniforms, meet registration and travel, the bill grows quickly. Multiply the new total by three and the burden on family finances becomes clear.

And we haven’t even accounted for her son Quinton’s high school football registration, which, at $300, is a relative bargain, or his rep basketball career, which ended early thanks to the $2,000 annual price tag.
Difficult decisions

“That’s why multisport isn’t a thing anymore once they reach a certain point,” says Jean-Pierre, who ran track at Brampton’s Turner-Fenton Secondary School in the early 2000s. “Now the one sport costs the same as if they were to do several sports.Track is $800 plus travel? It’s probably up to $1,200, $1,500 a year. I’m not doing that for three sports. Nor do I have the time.”

If we’re tracking the cost of keeping kids enrolled in multiple sports long enough for them to make more informed choices about how and when to specialize, we can also consider the Jean-Louis family fortunate. Other sports come with much steeper costs, along with difficult decisions about whether families can afford to raise well-rounded athletes.
A New Game Plan: The Norway Model

The 2025 Jumpstart study pegs the median cost of keeping a child enrolled in sports at $1,200. If the median is the midpoint, we know half of Canadian sports families spend more than $1,200 to keep their kids in the game. Many of them pay way more.

Witness the Marrero-Sinclairs, who pay roughly $4,000 per child, per year, to enroll their daughters in volleyball. Supplemental skills training, which they say many parents treat as essential, adds to their bill. Additional strength and conditioning training drives costs even higher.

Then there’s the cost of registering for, traveling to, and staying in hotels at tournaments during a club volleyball season that stretches from mid autumn to early spring. After that comes summer, where most players attend camps, which, the Merraro-Sinclairs say, can cost nearly $2,000 a week.
Sinclair says she doesn’t often pause to calculate the exact costs, but estimates that keeping two daughters enrolled in club volleyball can easily cost $14,000 a year.
“That’s the floor,” she says. “There’s no way that folks that grew up like Marlon and I would be making it on these teams. A) we couldn’t afford it and B) we couldn’t get there.”

Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders, seen during a Sports Illustrated photo shoot in 1989, is one of the most renowned multisport athletes, having played in both the National Football League and Major League Baseball. (Sports Illustrated)

Sports Illustrated’s first feature story on eventual NFL Hall of Famer Deion Sanders was published in July of 1989, and featured a full-page photo of the two-sport star standing outdoors, shirtless in the midday sun. Sanders was already playing pro baseball with the New York Yankees, but within a few weeks of this article he was scheduled to attend training camp with the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons. The only thing shinier than the lavish jheri curl atop his head is the gleaming gold chain around his neck. Sanders holds a baseball bat in his left hand and a football in his right. A heavy pendant in the shape of a dollar sign dangles at his sternum.

The story itself is about which sport Sanders would pursue professionally, and we couldn’t have known in 1989 that he would play both, at a high level, for a long time. But in 2026, the picture’s symbolism is hard to miss: two sports, one athlete, and a tug-of-war over money.
Sanders is, of course, an outlier.
It's possible for a star athlete to play nine seasons in MLB or 14 years in the NFL. Only Sanders managed both.
A New Game Plan: What Australia can teach Canada about rebuilding its sports system
Benefits to multisport participation

But he’s also just the most extreme version of the multisport athlete archetype. Sanders was a four-sport star in high school, and a three-sport standout at Florida State University before launching his pro careers. His MLB and NFL tenures didn’t just overlap with Bo Jackson’s time as an L.A. Raiders running back and Kansas City Royals outfielder. Sanders also spent his first three NFL seasons playing alongside Brian Jordan, who split time between the Falcons and St. Louis Cardinals minor-league teams before committing to baseball full-time in 1992.

Beyond those high-profile, dual-league professionals, multisport athletes often hide in plain sight. Before Michael Vick became a college football star, he was a Colorado Rockies baseball draftee. His Philadelphia Eagles teammate Desean Jackson was trending toward becoming an MLB draft pick, but made it clear as a high schooler that he preferred football.

Closer to home, the Canadian sprint record books are full of late bloomers and athletes who crossed over from other sports. Donovan Bailey and Andre De Grasse each, famously, started out as basketball players. Audrey Leduc, the second-fastest Canadian woman in history over 100 metres, was also a high-level soccer player who didn’t specialize in sprinting until university, and spent her childhood as a competitive trampoline athlete.
Audrey Leduc currently ranks among Canada's best sprinters, but she previously played high-level soccer as well. (Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images)
For his part Sanders attributes his success to the kind of athletic cross-pollination that happens when young athletes are able to play multiple sports for as long as possible.

“Kids should be all that they can be,” Sanders said in a video posted to YouTube. “Do all the things that you can do because statistics have shown that when a kid is engaged in multiple sports, normally their grade point average maintains itself.”

Sometimes the benefit is direct. Sanders’ iconic chasedown tackle of Don Beebe illustrates the difference between a fast NFL player and an NCAA sprinter with world-class talent. Beebe, the longtime Buffalo Bills special teams standout, is widely credited with a 4.2-second 40-yard dash time. Sanders also ran 4.2 before the NFL draft, but he was also a conference champion sprinter at Florida State, and on that play he flashed the 10.2 second 100-metre speed that only comes with dedicated track practice.

But experts also point out that sampling sports into adolescence produces long-term benefits, like co-ordination, general strength, and, crucially, the ability to pick up other skills. Veteran strength coach Clance Laylor says developing a broad sports foundation early helps athletes reach a higher peak later.

“You have this huge base, and when it’s time to specialize your adaptability is so much faster,” says Laylor, whose clients include former NHL star P.K. Subban, and who also coaches high-level weightlifters. “That’s why I get so excited when somebody wants to join my weightlifting team and I hear they’re a gymnast or a sprinter. Co-ordination, repetition. They’re neurologically more efficient. What you’re building is your brain, the capacity for your body to learn more movements.”

Sanders and his peers developed in the 1980s, when high schools offered a low-cost opportunity to play high-level sports, and when coaches understood that each sport had a distinct season. But in the current world of privatized youth sports, where costs accrue quickly, and coaches expect year-round commitment, athletes often become single-sport specialists by default.

“In high school it's also cheaper to try different sports, but that’s not the case anymore,” Jean-Louis says. “I can’t be like, ‘I wish you had what I had.’ We gotta move on. It is what it is, I guess.”
A New Game Plan: Sports Funding 101
As for solutions?

If we can’t bring youth athletics back to the multisport glory days, Laylor still offers some suggestions, like urging parents to abandon the FOMO that can prompt them to spend extra money on intensive year-round training. He advises cutting back on the costly extras that accompany a given sport, and investing that money in a second sport if your child is interested in playing. Switching sports a few times a year will help avoid mental and physical burnout, he says. And while the kids who specialize early develop more quickly, the athletes with a broad base of physical skills will close the gap quickly.

“Travel this, travel that… It’s a waste of time, and it’s expensive,” he says. “(Parents) are just forking out cash. For what? Work on your fundamentals, work on your technique. Once you hit puberty, those fundamentals, they’re gonna skyrocket. I’ve seen it so many times.”

Back at the Merraro-Sinclair household, 15-year-old Georgia is already absorbing those lessons. During middle school she wound down her martial arts career to focus on volleyball, but now she’s set to add flag football to her schedule. It’s a low-cost, low-pressure way to stay active, and sharpen some of the tools she’ll use on the volleyball court.
And most importantly, it’s social.
“I like competing and practicing with my friends,” Georgia says when asked what she likes most about playing sports.
Merraro breaks into a wide smile when he hears that Georgia still enjoys sport for sport’s sake. He turns and high-fives his daughter.
“That’s what I wanted to hear!” he says.
